# Simulation framework

This thesis uses an acceptance loop which has been further developed
from the loop described in @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL. In this section the
components of the loop are defined, i.e.

- The joint distribution $\mathbb{P}_{(Y, X)}$ of the repayment variable
  and the covariates,
- the acceptance decision $Z^{(t)}$ for each acceptance round, meaning formulating
    - the estimation method of the score function $s_t$,
    - the threshold calculation and
    - the complete decision function $d$ for both the MAR and MNAR cases
- from which the rest of the RVs and functions get formulated.

After defining each of the components an overview of the process as an algorithm
is provided.

## Applicants' population {#sec-app-population-simulation}

Recalling section @sec-measure-theoretic-desc-ri-problem, according to
the probabilistic model for the RL problem it suffices to define the
distributions of the repayment outcome and the features to define the applicants'
population. In the simulation I do not consider latent features (case $f_l = 0$).
Further let $\tilde{Y} := Y | \{\epsilon = \text{no external effect}\}$ denote
the "noiseless" repayment outcome. I describe the population with this variable,
since it is less convoluted, is the object that the scorecard will
attempt to model and is easily bridged to the idea of a good and bad applicants.
It holds $\tilde{Y} \sim Bernoulli(\pi_{b})$ with $\pi_b \in (0,1)$
the probability of a bad applicant. The observable features vector $X$^[
    Recall from @eq-X-joint-observable-feats-vec: $X = \left(X_m^{\top}, X_h^{\top} \right)^{\top}$
]
is defined as a Gaussian Mixture with two components, a good one (paying population)
and a bad one (defaulters). With $o \in \{g, b\}$ we can characterize the distributions
of these populations as
$$
X | \{\tilde{Y}=o\} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(
    \mu_o =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \mu_{m, o} \\ \mu_{h, o}
    \end{pmatrix},
    \Sigma_o =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \Sigma_{m, o} & \Sigma_{mh, o} \\
        \Sigma_{mh, o}^{\top} & \Sigma_{h, o}
    \end{pmatrix}
\right)
$$
with $\Sigma_o, \Sigma_{m, o}$ and $\Sigma_{h, o}$ strictly positive definite (so, non-singular).
Letting $X_o$ be short for $X | \{\tilde{Y}=o\}$ also let $\phi_{X_o}$ denote its probability density
function (pdf). Since $X_o$ is normally distributed the pdf is given by
$$
\phi_{X_o}(x) := 
\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^f |\Sigma_o|} }
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu_o)^\top \Sigma_o^{-1} (x-\mu_o)\right\}
$$

For further analysis it is also helpful to write down the characterization of the joint distribution
of $(X,\tilde{Y})$, which is the marginal distribution of $\mathbb{P}_{X_m, X_h, X_l, Y}$ over the latent
feature component, given $\epsilon = \text{no external effect}$. Its density^[
    Following @Pollard_2001 [Ch. 3, Sec. 1], densities are understood here in the Radon–Nikodym sense,
    such that absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue measure alone is not required, but can be
    given with respect to any dominating measure.
] is defined as a Radon-Nikodym derivative, using that the normal distribution is absolutely continuous
w. r. t. the Lebesgue Measure, in this case $\lambda^f$ over $\mathbb{R}^f$, and the discreteness of $Y$
$$
p_{X, \tilde{Y}} = \frac{d\mathbb{P}_{X, \tilde{Y}}}{d\left(\lambda^f \otimes \#_Y\right)}
$$
where $\#_Y$ is the counting measure over $E_Y$, which gets evaluated pointwise as a map
$\mathbb{R}^f \times E_y \to [0, \infty)$
$$
p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, o) = \pi_o \cdot \phi_{X_o}(x)
$$
where $\pi_g := 1 - \pi_b$.

From this we can easily derive the marginals^[
    Since $\pi_b \in (0, 1)$ and $\phi_{X_o}$ is strictly positive *and*
    finite everywhere, the marginal densities of $\mathbb{P}_{X, \tilde{Y}}$ over
    $X$ and $\tilde{Y}$ each are well-defined [@Pollard_2001, Ch. 4, Theorem 12]
] as
$$
p_{\tilde{Y}}(o) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{f}} p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, o) \, \lambda^f(dx) = \pi_o ,
$${#eq-marginal-of-Y}
which of course corresponds to the probability mass function of a Bernoulli
distributed variable, and
$$
p_X(x) = \int_{E_Y} p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, y) \, \#_{Y}(dy) = \pi_b \phi_{X_b}(x) + \pi_g \phi_{X_g}(x)
$${#eq-marginal-of-X}

which is the pdf of a Gaussian Mixture and thus finally:
$$
\mathbb{P}(\tilde{Y} = o | X=x) = p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (o, x) = \frac{\phi_{X_o}(x) p_{\tilde{Y}}(o)}{p_X(x)}
$${#eq-posterior-of-Y}

With $o=b$ @eq-posterior-of-Y returns the object that $s_t$ should model. See that this
objective also excludes overfitting, as no noise is modeled here. Now
let us assume that $\epsilon, \varepsilon$ are Bernoulli distributed
with parameters $\pi_{\epsilon} := \mathbb{P}(\epsilon =\text{no idiosyncratic shock}) > 0$
and $\pi_{\varepsilon, b} := \mathbb{P}(\varepsilon = b) \in (0,1)$. 
With this we can further write down
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y = b | X = x) = p_{Y=b | X}(x) = 
    \pi_{\epsilon} \, p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (b, x) +
    (1 - \pi_{\epsilon}) \pi_{\varepsilon, b}
$${#eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes}
which is the basis for the best possible prediction of a bad loan.

It becomes quickly clear that the amount of metaparameters for the
simulation is overwhelming, so that for a comparable study a relatively
simple setting has been selected. Namely $f_m = 2$, $f_h = 0$,
$\Sigma_g = \Sigma_b = \Sigma$ and $\Sigma_{mh}^\top = \sigma_{mh} \mathbf{1}_{f_m \times f_h}$
with $\mathbf{1}_{f_m \times f_h} \in \mathbb{R}^{f_m \times f_h}$ a matrix
of ones and $\sigma_{mh} \in \mathbb{R}$. Therefore the distributional
differences between $X_o$ and $X_g$ are solely characterized by the mean difference. Their distributions are given by:
```{python}
#| notebook-links: false
```

Its Bayes Error rate is `{python} bayes_err_str`$\%$. We can see a
visualization of the complete dgp in @fig-3d-base-dgp, whereby the Perfect Bayes Boundary
corresponds to the classification boundary of a classifier given by 
@eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes. This boundary is calculated in the appendix
(see @sec-dec-boundary-perf-bayes-idyiosincratic-shocks) and can be
rewritten from @eq-decision-boundary-equal-covs as the hyperplane
$$
W x - \beta = \log c
$${#eq-hyperplane-decision-boundary}
with $W=(\mu_b - \mu_g)^\top \Sigma^{-1} = \Sigma^{-1}(\mu_b - \mu_g)$,
$\beta = W\frac{\mu_b + \mu_g}{2}$ and $c$ a real constant depending on
the idyiosincratic schock dynamics ($\pi_{\epsilon}$ and $\pi_{\varepsilon, b}$)
and the unconditional probability of default ($\pi_b$).

```{python}
#| label: fig-3d-base-dgp
#| fig-cap: "Representation of joint distribution $(Y, X)$"
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from itertools import combinations
from math import log
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

inv_cov = torch.cholesky_inverse(dgp_base.bad_mixture.cov_chol_decomp)
mu_b = dgp_base.bad_mixture.mean
mu_g = dgp_base.good_mixture.mean
pi_b = dgp_base.prob_bad_given_no_shock

# --- Precompute everything once ---
W = inv_cov @ (mu_b - mu_g)

beta = W @ ((mu_b + mu_g)/2)

c = (1-pi_b)/pi_b

if dgp_base.simulate_idiosyncratic_shocks:
    # --- Compute noisy shift ---
    pi_eps = 1 - dgp_base.prob_idiosyncratic_shock
    pi_vareps_b = dgp_base.prob_bad_given_shock

    xi = (0.5 - (1-pi_eps)*pi_vareps_b) / pi_eps
    c *= xi / (1-xi)

bias = beta + log(c)   # final intercept

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12,4.5))

ax = fig.add_subplot(1,1, 1, projection="3d")

ellipsoid_probs = (.8,)
dgp_base.plot_credit_dgp_3d(
    sample_size=10_000,
    axes=[ax], elev=15, azim=-10,
    ellipsoid_probs=ellipsoid_probs
)
#pos = ax.get_position()
ax.set_box_aspect((4, 5, 3))

inv_cov = torch.cholesky_inverse(dgp_base.bad_mixture.cov_chol_decomp)
mu_b = dgp_base.bad_mixture.mean
mu_g = dgp_base.good_mixture.mean
pi = dgp_base.prob_bad_given_no_shock


# --- Compute LDA direction ---
# --- Create grid for plane ---
xx, yy = torch.meshgrid(
    torch.linspace(-2, 3, 30),
    torch.linspace(-1.2, 3, 30),
    indexing="xy"
)

# Solve for z: w1*x + w2*y + w3*z + b = 0
zz = (bias - W[0]*xx - W[1]*yy) / W[2]

# Convert to numpy for matplotlib
xx_np = xx.numpy()
yy_np = yy.numpy()
zz_np = zz.numpy()

# --- Plot the plane ---
surf = ax.plot_surface(xx_np, yy_np, zz_np, alpha=0.3, color="black", label="Perf. Bayes boundary")

# --- Create a proxy artist for the legend ---
# We match the facecolor (black) and alpha (0.3) of the surface

# --- Append to existing legend handles ---
# 1. Grab what is already in the legend (from dgp_base plot)
handles, labels = [], []
for handle, label in zip(*ax.get_legend_handles_labels()):
    if label not in labels:
        handles.append(handle)
        labels.append(label)

# 2. Append your new proxy artist and its label
#handles.append(surface_proxy)
#labels.append("Perf. Bayes boundary")
#fig.legends.append()

fig.legend(
    handles=[surf],
    labels=["Perf. Bayes boundary"],
    loc='lower center',
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0),
    ncol=max(1, min(len(handles), 4)),
    frameon=False,
    fontsize=9,
    handlelength=1.5,
    columnspacing=1.2
)


ax.set_xlabel("$X_{m, 1}$")
ax.set_ylabel("$X_{m, 2}$")
ax.set_zlabel("$X_{h}$")

pos = ax.get_position()
ax.set_position([pos.x0 - 0.1, pos.y0 - 0.05, pos.width + 0.12, pos.height])


plt.show()
```

Considering the bayes error rate of the problem, the good separability by the
hyperplane of the perfect bayes decision boundary observable in @fig-3d-base-dgp,
it is clear that a logit model (which also has a linear discriminant) with no
missing variable bias, should have no problem estimating a good classifier. To check
out how difficult the problem gets while ignoring one of the variables, a pairwise
component plot as in @fig-pairwise-base-dgp is a good diagnostic. There the perfect
bayes boundary was calculated using the hyperplane described in @eq-hyperplane-decision-boundary,
whereby the non considered component of the features in each plot was set to its
expected value of $X$ given no shock. Meaning with $r$ component's position in $X$ of the
non-shown component, it was set in @eq-hyperplane-decision-boundary
$$
x\mathtt{[r]} = \mathbb{E}(X | \epsilon = \text{no shock})\mathtt{[r]} = (\pi_b)\mu_b\mathtt{[r]} + (1-\pi_b)\mu_g\mathtt{[r]}
$$

It is clear that @fig-pairwise-base-dgp also suggests that the classification
problem shoud also be well solved by a logistic regression considering only two
of the components of $X$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pairwise-base-dgp
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise covariates component representation of $Y, X$"
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12,4.5))
F = dgp_base.F
aes_dict = {}
lbl_maker = lambda f: f"$X_{{m, {f+1}}}$" if f < F-1 else "$X_{h}$"
for (f1, f2), a_idx in zip(combinations(range(F), 2), range(1, 4)):
    aes_dict[f"{f1:02}{f2:02}"] = fig.add_subplot(1,3, a_idx)
    aes_dict[f"{f1:02}{f2:02}"].set_xlabel(lbl_maker(f1))
    aes_dict[f"{f1:02}{f2:02}"].set_ylabel(lbl_maker(f2))

_, handles_2d, legends_2d = dgp_base.pairwise_plot_dgp(
    sample_size=18_000, axes=[aes_dict]
)

# --- Add decision boundary to each 2D subplot ---
# --- Add decision boundary to each 2D subplot ---
f_all = set(range(F))
for (f1, f2), a_idx in zip(combinations(range(F), 2), range(1, 4)):
    ax = aes_dict[f"{f1:02}{f2:02}"]

    # pick the remaining coordinate index
    f3 = list(f_all - {f1, f2})[0]

    # grid for x_f1
    x1_vals = torch.linspace(-1.5, 3, 200) if f1==1 and f2==2 else torch.linspace(*ax.get_xlim(), 200)

    # FIXED VALUE FOR THE UNPLOTTED COORDINATE
    x3_fixed = (1 - pi_b) * mu_g[f3] + pi_b * mu_b[f3]

    # compute x_f2 from plane equation
    x2_vals = (bias - W[f1] * x1_vals - W[f3] * x3_fixed) / W[f2]

    line, = ax.plot(x1_vals.numpy(), x2_vals.numpy(), color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)


fig.legend(
    handles_2d + [line],
    legends_2d + ["Perf. Bayes boundary"],
    loc='lower center',
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.07),
    ncol=len(handles_2d) + 1,
    frameon=False,
    fontsize=10,
    handlelength=1.5,
    columnspacing=1.2
)

fig.tight_layout()

plt.show()
```

## Decision and scoring functions

The decision function has two phases, the starting phase (where no data has been gathered yet)
and the scoring function estimating phase. In the following is explained how in each moment
the function looks like.

\end{cases}
